title: Adab with creation
hook: a cat shut in and left hungry, a dog at a well, and a leather sock full of water

segments.voice: Yesterday, adab with children, and your line: mercy for mercy. Did one child get your full attention? Today, mercy reaches past people altogether. Day one thousand three hundred four.

A cat, shut in. No food set down. And no way out to hunt for its own. That's the whole story, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, in paraphrase: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said a woman entered the Fire because of a cat. She neither fed it nor let it loose to eat the small creatures of the earth. No crime against a person. No grand sin anyone would whisper about. One animal, in her power, and ignored. Today: the manners owed to everything that breathes.
screen: `A CAT, SHUT IN.` → `NOT FED. NOT FREED.` → `ONE ANIMAL, IN HER POWER.`

segments.voice: Start with the Qur'an's view of animals. Surah al-An'am, in Pickthall's translation: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you." Peoples. Communities with their own lives, not furniture in ours. Then put the cat beside a second story, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase. A man walking along a road grew desperately thirsty. He found a well, climbed down, and drank. Climbing out, he saw a dog panting, licking damp earth from thirst. He thought: this dog is suffering what I just suffered. So he went back down, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb, and gave the dog a drink. And the Prophet said Allah thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions were surprised. They asked: is there reward for us even in animals? His answer, in paraphrase: in every living thing with a moist liver, there is reward. A moist liver. A body that is alive. That's the whole qualification. Set the two stories side by side and they mirror each other. One person had an animal in her control and did nothing. One person had no duty to a stray dog at all, and went back down the well. Adab with creation lives in that space between. Not a theory about animals. The choice, when something weaker is thirsty in front of you, to notice it, the way the man noticed: this is what I just felt.
screen: `AL-AN'AM: PEOPLES LIKE UNTO YOU.` · `A DOG AT THE WELL.` · `A MOIST LIVER, A REWARD.` · `TWO STORIES, ONE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the animals that cross your day. A pet asleep on the couch. Pigeons at the bus stop. A stray cat under a parked car. The squirrel in the yard. Choose one. Ask the man's question at the well: what does this creature need that I happen to have? Water in a bowl by the door. Crumbs for birds, where it's allowed. A fresh dish for your own animal, set down with attention. If you pray, you can remember that creature in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Adab with creation. The manners owed to every living thing: not leaving it hungry in your power, and going back down the well when it's thirsty. Today's word.
Your line: every creature counts. Today, feed a stray or set out water, or simply refill your own animal's bowl with care. Tomorrow, adab with the earth. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: Islamic teaching on animals draws on Qur'an 6:38, which calls animals and birds peoples like us, and on hadith such as the woman and the cat and the man who gave water to a thirsty dog.

original.note: Arabic: a moist liver, the hadith's phrase for any living thing.

trapdoor: what you thought: adab with creation means being nice to pets.
what it means: what you owe any living thing in your reach: not leaving it hungry, going back for it when it's thirsty.
what a scholar hears: 'in every moist liver there is reward' (Bukhari 2363), and al-An'am 6:38: animals and birds are peoples like you.
